title: Find the Largest Almost Missing Integer
statement: Look at every contiguous block of exactly `k` elements of `nums` (there are `nums.length - k + 1` such windows). Call a value `x` *almost missing* when precisely one of these windows contains `x` (once or more). Return the largest almost missing value, or `-1` if no value is almost missing.
notes:
## Intuition

The direct way counts, for every value, the windows that contain it: O(n · k). Counting windows per index is quicker to reason about: index `i` lies in every window that starts between `max(0, i - k + 1)` and `min(i, n - k)`. Three cases follow.

- `k = n`: there is one window, so every value is in exactly one window and the answer is the maximum.
- `k = 1`: each window is one element, so a value is in as many windows as it has copies. The answer is the largest value seen exactly once.
- Otherwise every inner index lies in at least two windows, and only `nums[0]` (first window) and `nums[n - 1]` (last window) lie in one. An end value qualifies only if it occurs nowhere else: another copy is either inside, in two windows, or at the other end, in a different window.

All of this needs only how often each value occurs.

## Approach

1. If `k === n`, return the largest value.
2. Count every value's occurrences in `count` (values are 0 to 50).
3. If `k === 1`, scan values from 50 down and return the first with a count of 1, or `-1`.
4. Otherwise start `best` at `-1` and offer `nums[0]` and `nums[n - 1]`, each only if its count is 1.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [3, 9, 2, 1, 7]`, `k = 3`, `n = 5`. Neither special case applies. Every value occurs once. `nums[0] = 3` has count 1, so `best = 3`; `nums[4] = 7` has count 1, so `best = max(3, 7) = 7`, the answer.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + 51): one counting pass and at most one scan of the 51 possible values.
- Space: O(51) for `count`.

## Pitfalls

- The largest value overall is not the answer: in Test 8, 9 sits in the middle and lies in all three windows.
- An end value may have another copy: in Test 7 both ends hold 8, which is in the first and the last window, so the answer is `-1`.
- With `k = n` even repeated values qualify (Test 4); with `k = 1` they never do (Example 3).

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `count[value]` | how many times `value` occurs in `nums` |
| `value` | a value being counted or scanned |
| `best` | largest almost missing value found, or `-1` |

narration.4: The largest value of the whole array is then the answer.
narration.6: Values are between 0 and 50, so a plain array can count them.
narration.8: Count how many times this value occurs.
narration.10: With k = 1 each window is one element, so a value is in as many windows as it has copies.
narration.11: Scan values from the top so the first hit is the largest.
narration.12: Exactly one copy means exactly one window.
narration.16: Every value repeats, so none is almost missing.
narration.18: Otherwise only the two end elements sit in a single window; start with no answer.
narration.19: The first element is almost missing only if its value occurs nowhere else.
narration.22: The same test for the last element.
narration.23: Keep the larger of the two candidates.
narration.25: Return the best candidate, or -1 if neither end qualified.
